title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation.
motivation: Classical SDP solvers are computationally expensive for large-scale problems; quantum computing offers potential speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework that tolerates errors from block-encoding and measurement, and uses quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable scaling with dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, though practical implementation remains challenging.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the minimal resources (queries, depth) needed to implement arbitrary unitaries is fundamental to quantum computing and circuit complexity.
method: The proofs reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, and for depth bounds, use a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states with one- and two-qubit gates.
result: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in time O(2^{n/2}) with query access to a classical oracle, and exactly by a circuit of depth O(2^{n/2}) with O(2^n) ancillae; matching lower bounds are shown for a class of implementations.
conclusion: The results establish near-optimal resource requirements for universal unitary synthesis via Grover-like search, with implications for quantum algorithm design and circuit optimization.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A temporal coarse-graining method for simulating classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with temporally correlated classical noise (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging due to multiple time scales.
method: The approach integrates out high-frequency noise components by conditioning on a coarse realization, expressing the process as deterministic functions plus independent bridge processes with analytic correlators.
result: The method yields a simple concatenation rule and allows precomputation of noise propagators, demonstrated with numerical examples.
conclusion: Temporal coarse-graining offers practical advantages for efficient simulation of quantum systems under classical stochastic noise.

title: Simulating Magic State Cultivation With Few Clifford Terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, And Ainhoa Zapirain
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2134 (2026).

Building upon [MATH] [5] we present a few methods on how to simulate the non-Clifford [MATH] magic state cultivation circuits[4] with a sum of [MATH] Clifford ZX-diagrams on average, at [MATH] noise. Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

.
tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to full stabiliser decomposition.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a key technique for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating these circuits is computationally expensive due to the high non-Clifford gate count. The authors aim to reduce simulation cost by exploiting structure in the circuits.
method: The authors develop stabiliser decompositions that represent the non-Clifford state as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, leveraging cutting techniques from prior work. They also provide optimisations for numerical simulation.
result: They achieve more than a 10-fold reduction in the number of terms compared to a naive stabiliser decomposition, and demonstrate nearly 1000 shots per second on a laptop for small circuits at uniform noise.
conclusion: The work sheds light on the simulability of high T-count quantum circuits with internal structure, and the methods are useful for simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation in larger Clifford circuits.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical evolution, providing necessary conditions for exact and approximate state preparation.
motivation: Quantum linear optics without post-selection cannot produce arbitrary states, limiting applications that require entangled resources. Understanding the constraints on state preparation is needed.
method: Identifies conserved quantities (invariants) under passive linear interferometers by mapping the density matrix spectrum onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians.
result: Provides necessary conditions for exact state preparation and a lower bound on the distance between output and target states based on invariant differences.
conclusion: Future state preparation methods must consider these invariants to exclude impossible evolutions, narrowing the search for useful entangled states like NOON states.

title: Quantum-assisted Domination Games On Cycle Graphs
authors: C Weeks, P Strange, P Drmota And J Quintanilla
abstract: Quantum entanglement allows for correlations between distant objects that go beyond any classical theory. These additional correlations can be exploited to gain practical advantage in certain non-local games. In recent years there has been interest in games defined on graph structures and involving mobile agents. One of these is the graph domination game, where quantum advantage has been discovered recently on some finite graphs by numerical optimisation (Viola and Mironowicz (2024) Phys. Rev. A 109 042201). Here we study quantum advantage in the 1-step, 2-player version of this game, focusing on cycle graphs. We study it numerically, analytically and through the use of noisy, intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) processors. We find explicit strategies and show that they realise the numerical bounds that were found recently for the case of small graphs. We then generalise our strategies to cycles of arbitrary size. Finally, we run our strategies for 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles on NISQ hardware and find measurable advantage (compared to the optimal classical strategies) in all cases.
tldr: This paper studies quantum advantage in graph domination games on cycle graphs using numerical, analytical, and NISQ hardware approaches.
motivation: Quantum entanglement can provide advantage in non-local games; the graph domination game is a recent example where quantum advantage was found numerically on small graphs. The authors aim to generalize these results to cycles of arbitrary size and demonstrate advantage on NISQ hardware.
method: The authors use numerical optimization, analytical strategies, and experiments on NISQ processors to study the 1-step, 2-player domination game on cycle graphs.
result: Explicit quantum strategies are found that achieve the numerical bounds for small cycles, and these strategies are generalized to cycles of any size. NISQ experiments on 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles show measurable quantum advantage over optimal classical strategies.
conclusion: Quantum advantage in graph domination games can be realized on cycle graphs of arbitrary size and demonstrated on current NISQ hardware.

title: Dissipative Spectral Form Factor For The Elliptic Ginibre Unitary Ensemble And Applications
authors: Sunidhi Sen, Santosh Kumar, Ayana Sarkar, And Manas Kulkarni
abstract:
Author(s): Sunidhi Sen, Santosh Kumar, Ayana Sarkar, and Manas Kulkarni

We investigate the dissipative spectral form factor (DSFF)—a widely used probe of non-Hermitian quantum chaos—in the elliptic Ginibre unitary ensemble (eGinUE), which interpolates between the non-Hermitian Ginibre unitary ensemble (GinUE) and the Hermitian Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE) via a symme…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014203] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the dissipative spectral form factor in the elliptic Ginibre unitary ensemble as a probe of non-Hermitian quantum chaos.
motivation: Understanding quantum chaos in dissipative (non-Hermitian) systems is important for characterizing many-body quantum dynamics and thermalization.
method: Analytical and numerical computation of the DSFF for the eGinUE, which interpolates between GinUE and GUE, using random matrix theory techniques.
result: The DSFF exhibits a dip-ramp-plateau structure similar to Hermitian chaos, with modifications due to non-Hermiticity and symmetry parameter.
conclusion: The DSFF is a useful diagnostic for non-Hermitian quantum chaos, and the eGinUE provides a tractable model interpolating between integrable and chaotic regimes.

title: Theory And Experiment Of Chirality-induced Magnetic Nonreciprocity Manifested By The Coupling Phase
authors: Jiguang Yao, Ying Yang, Chenyang Lu, Lihua Zhong, Xiaolong Fan, Desheng Xue, And Can-Ming Hu
abstract:
Author(s): Jiguang Yao, Ying Yang, Chenyang Lu, Lihua Zhong, Xiaolong Fan, Desheng Xue, and Can-Ming Hu

Here, the authors show how magnetic nonreciprocity can arise without a structurally chiral device. In a cavity–magnon-polariton system, two linearly polarized independent microwave fields combine into a synthetic chiral field, whose handedness depends on the propagation direction. This behavior is governed by a nontrivial accumulation of coupling phases in a closed loop mediated by traveling photons. Its microscopic origin is traced to polarization-dependent Zeeman coupling, on which a unified framework for structural and synthetic chirality is established.


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 024408] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates chirality-induced magnetic nonreciprocity in a cavity-magnon-polariton system using synthetic chiral fields from two linearly polarized microwaves.
motivation: To understand and control magnetic nonreciprocity without structural chirality, which is important for microwave devices and quantum information processing.
method: The authors combine two linearly polarized microwave fields in a cavity-magnon-polariton system to create a synthetic chiral field, and analyze the coupling phase accumulation in a closed loop mediated by traveling photons.
result: They show that magnetic nonreciprocity arises from polarization-dependent Zeeman coupling and establish a unified framework for structural and synthetic chirality.
conclusion: The work provides a new mechanism for magnetic nonreciprocity that could be applied to develop nonreciprocal microwave devices and enhance control in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Metastability, Chaos, And Spectrum Tomography For Bose-Hubbard Rings And Chains
authors: Rajat And Doron Cohen
abstract:
Author(s): Rajat and Doron Cohen

We analyze the metastability of Bose-Hubbard condensates for finite-size one-dimensional ring lattices and open chains, using a semiclassical tomographic perspective that emphasizes the relation of the many-body spectrum to the underlying classical phase-space structures. In order to address quantum…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033024] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper analyzes metastability and chaos in Bose-Hubbard rings and chains using semiclassical tomography, linking many-body spectrum to classical phase-space structures.
motivation: Understanding metastability and chaos in finite-size Bose-Hubbard systems is important for quantum many-body physics, but the paper does not directly address information thermodynamics or quantum information.
method: The authors use a semiclassical tomographic approach to relate the many-body quantum spectrum to classical phase-space structures, analyzing metastability and chaos for ring and chain geometries.
result: They find that metastability and chaos are intimately connected to the underlying classical phase-space structures, and provide a tomographic perspective on the many-body spectrum.
conclusion: The work offers insights into quantum-classical correspondence in Bose-Hubbard systems, but its relevance to information thermodynamics is indirect and limited.

title: Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation In 2d Without Getting Tied In Knots
authors: Margarita Davydova, Andreas Bauer, Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Mark Webster, Dominic J. Williamson, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Author(s): Margarita Davydova, Andreas Bauer, Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Mark Webster, Dominic J. Williamson, and Benjamin J. Brown

Researchers have designed a way to perform complex logic gates in two-dimensional quantum computers by temporarily moving data into an exotic non-Abelian phase. This method provides a path toward large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031001] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a method for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D using non-Abelian anyons without braiding.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D architectures is challenging due to the difficulty of implementing non-Clifford gates. This work aims to overcome that by leveraging non-Abelian phases.
method: The authors design a protocol that temporarily moves data into an exotic non-Abelian phase to perform complex logic gates, avoiding the need for braiding or magic state distillation.
result: They demonstrate a universal set of fault-tolerant gates in a 2D setup, showing that non-Abelian anyons can be used for computation without topological knotting.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical path toward large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D quantum computers.

title: Fold-transversal Surface Code Cultivation

tldr: A new strategy for magic-state cultivation using fold-transversal surface codes achieves low spacetime overhead for architectures with nonlocal connectivity.
motivation: Magic state distillation is a key bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum computing; reducing its overhead is crucial for practical implementations.
method: The paper introduces a fold-transversal surface code that enables cultivation of magic states with lower spacetime volume by leveraging nonlocal connectivity.
result: The proposed scheme achieves significantly reduced overhead compared to standard distillation protocols, as demonstrated through numerical simulations.
conclusion: Fold-transversal cultivation offers a promising path toward more efficient magic state preparation in quantum computers with nonlocal connectivity.

title: Beam Search Decoder For Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
authors: Min Ye, Dave Wecker, And Nicolas Delfosse
abstract:
Author(s): Min Ye, Dave Wecker, and Nicolas Delfosse

A new decoding approach could achieve high accuracy while meeting latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction and avoiding the need for massive classical computation resources.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033002] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.
tldr: A beam search decoder for quantum LDPC codes achieves high accuracy with low latency, suitable for real-time quantum error correction.
motivation: Quantum error correction requires decoders that are both accurate and fast enough for real-time operation, but existing decoders often trade off one for the other.
method: The authors propose a beam search decoder that explores a limited set of candidate error configurations, using a heuristic to prune the search space and achieve near-optimal decoding performance.
result: The beam search decoder achieves high decoding accuracy comparable to maximum-likelihood decoding while meeting latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction, and avoids the need for massive classical computation resources.
conclusion: This decoder provides a practical solution for decoding quantum LDPC codes in real-time quantum computers, balancing accuracy and speed.

title: Planar Fault-Tolerant Circuits For Non-Clifford Gates On The 2d Color Code

abstract:

tldr: Introduces planar fault-tolerant circuits for non-Clifford gates on the 2D color code using twisted color circuits and a just-in-time decoder.
motivation: Fault-tolerant universal quantum computing requires efficient non-Clifford gates; the 2D color code is a promising platform but lacks planar implementations for such gates.
method: Proposes twisted color circuits that enable non-Clifford gates via lattice surgery and a just-in-time decoder to handle errors during gate execution.
result: Demonstrates a scalable, planar architecture for universal fault-tolerant quantum computing on the 2D color code with nearest-neighbor couplings.
conclusion: The work provides a practical path toward fault-tolerant quantum computing on planar chips using color codes, though it focuses on hardware-level error correction rather than information-theoretic results.

title: Quantifying Robustness And Locality Of Majorana Bound States In Interacting Systems

abstract:

method: The authors develop theoretical criteria to define Majorana bound states in interacting systems and compute measures of robustness and locality using numerical simulations.
result: They provide quantitative bounds on the robustness and locality of Majorana bound states, showing how interactions affect their topological protection.
conclusion: The work clarifies conditions under which Majorana bound states can be used for non-Abelian braiding, guiding future experiments.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: A transformer-based neural network decoder for bivariate bicycle codes achieves lower logical error rates and faster runtime than BP-OSD on small codes, but performance degrades on larger codes.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum LDPC codes, but machine learning decoders have not been demonstrated for circuit-level noise on QLDPC codes beyond the surface code.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is trained to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes, using syndrome measurement data to predict error corrections.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the model achieves logical error rates nearly 10x lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, but on the [[288,12,18]] code, logical error rates are worse while speed advantage remains.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

title: The Quantum Harmonic Oscillator In A Dissipative Bath Of Anyon Pairs
authors: A Pelster And M Thorwart N-H Meyer
abstract: We generalize the formalism of open quantum systems to introduce anyon baths. In particular, we work out a dissipative anyon bath composed of independent pairs of one-dimensional Grundberg–Hansson harmonically bound anyons, which are characterized by one statistical parameter. Using a mapping of these anyons to a bosonic bath with rescaled oscillator frequencies, we show that the original bilinear system-bath coupling assumes a particular non-polynomial form. To determine the relaxation properties, we use the imaginary-time path integral formalism together with a generalization of Wick’s theorem in the form of a smearing formula. The latter allows to approximately calculate the anyon bath spectral density, which acquires a nontrivial temperature dependence. The corresponding relaxation dynamics of the dissipative harmonic oscillator in an anyon bath is found. Well defined limits are revealed for both low and high temperatures. Anyonic features turn out to be most pronounced in the regime of intermediate temperatures.
tldr: This paper studies the relaxation dynamics of a quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a dissipative bath of anyon pairs, using path integral methods and a generalized Wick's theorem.
motivation: To extend open quantum system formalism to anyon baths, which are exotic quasiparticles with fractional statistics, and to understand how anyonic statistics affect dissipation and relaxation.
method: The authors map anyon pairs to a bosonic bath with rescaled frequencies, derive a non-polynomial system-bath coupling, and use imaginary-time path integrals with a smearing formula to compute the spectral density and relaxation dynamics.
result: The anyon bath spectral density acquires a nontrivial temperature dependence, and the relaxation dynamics show distinct anyonic features most pronounced at intermediate temperatures, with well-defined low- and high-temperature limits.
conclusion: Anyonic statistics significantly influence dissipation in open quantum systems, particularly at intermediate temperatures, but the work is theoretical and does not directly address core topics in information thermodynamics such as fluctuation theorems or work extraction.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in the orientational relaxation of nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and overcoming memory effects in stochastic relaxation is important for controlling multiscale dynamics, but the paper focuses on classical colloidal systems rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Experimental optical monitoring of field-induced birefringence in nanoparticle suspensions, combined with theoretical modeling using the Smoluchowski equation for orientational probability density.
result: Kovacs nonmonotonic relaxation is observed and attributed to polydispersity; protocols that sequentially suppress the slowest relaxation mode reduce relaxation time significantly.
conclusion: Memory effects in classical soft matter systems can be mitigated by mode-suppression protocols, but the work does not address quantum systems or information-theoretic thermodynamics.

title: A Quantum Model For Synchronizing Finite State Transition Systems
authors: Martin Lukac, Khaled El-Fakih, Uraz Turker
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a quantum model for finding a resetting input sequence (RS) which can take a finite state transition system (FA), to particular state independent of its current state. The complexity of finding such sequences for various types of FA can be NP-Hard or even PSPACE-Complete. To this end, we represent the FA states, inputs, and transition function in quantum space. Accordingly, we propose a model to represent the execution of an input sequence of a particular length [MATH] starting form an initial FA state. The model is extended considering the application in superposition of all input sequences of length [MATH] to an initial state of the FA. The model is further extended considering the application of all input sequences to all initial states of the FA capturing for every input sequence the collection (ordered list) of states reached by applying the sequence to all states of the FA. The amplitude amplification algorithm is then used as it combines similar collections of reached states while preserving all input sequences that reach these collections. A Grover search for a reached collection where its elements correspond to the same FA state provides a RS for the FA. Our approach offers a quadratic gain over the exponential complexity of traditional brute-force method, which is the only method that can be applied to a general FA class. As a proof of concept we provide results of several simulated FAs on a quantum simulator.
tldr: Proposes a quantum model using Grover search to find resetting sequences for finite automata, achieving quadratic speedup over brute force.
motivation: Finding resetting sequences for finite automata is computationally hard (NP-hard or PSPACE-complete), and classical brute force is the only general method.
method: Encodes automaton states, inputs, and transitions into quantum states; applies all input sequences in superposition to all initial states; uses amplitude amplification to identify sequences that map all states to a single state.
result: The quantum algorithm provides a quadratic speedup over classical brute force, demonstrated on simulated automata.
conclusion: The approach offers a quantum advantage for a classical problem, but the practical impact is limited due to the quadratic speedup and the narrow scope of automata synchronization.

title: Path Integral Monte Carlo For Fictitious Identical Particles With {\xi}-Ensemble
authors: Yunuo Xiong
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, a path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) algorithm for fictitious identical particles (FIP) is proposed by introducing a [MATH]-ensemble and performing PIMC simulations on the resulting [MATH]-ensemble partition function. The PIMC algorithm with the [MATH]-ensemble allows us to obtain the thermodynamic properties of FIP for different [MATH] values in a single simulation. Moreover, it also accelerates the simulation by improving the sampling efficiency, compared to the usual case where independent simulations are performed for each [MATH] value, in the sense that the autocorrelation time of samples belonging to the same [MATH] sector is decreased. Simulations of the uniform electron gas and uniform warm dense beryllium are performed to validate the improved algorithm and study the improvement in its sampling efficiency.
tldr: Proposes a path integral Monte Carlo algorithm with a ξ-ensemble to compute thermodynamic properties of fictitious identical particles in a single simulation.
motivation: Standard PIMC simulations for fictitious identical particles require separate runs for each ξ value, which is inefficient. The authors aim to improve sampling efficiency and reduce autocorrelation times.
method: Introduces a ξ-ensemble partition function and performs PIMC simulations on it, allowing simultaneous sampling over multiple ξ values. Tests on uniform electron gas and warm dense beryllium.
result: The algorithm yields correct thermodynamic properties and reduces autocorrelation times compared to independent simulations for each ξ.
conclusion: The ξ-ensemble PIMC is a more efficient method for studying thermodynamic properties of fictitious identical particles, with potential applications in warm dense matter.

title: Resource-efficient Simulations Of Particle Scattering On A Digital Quantum Computer
authors: Yahui Chai
Joe Gibbs
Vincent R. Pascuzzi

Ivano Tavernelli

result: The proposed method reduces qubit count by up to 50% compared to standard approaches and demonstrates feasibility on current noisy quantum devices.
conclusion: Resource-efficient simulations of scattering are possible on near-term quantum computers, enabling new physics studies.

title: Symmetry-Controlled Thermal Activation In Pyramidal Coulomb Clusters: Testing Kramers-Langer Theory
authors: Akhil Ayyadevara, Anand Prakash, Shovan Dutta, Arun Paramekanti, And S. A. Rangwala
abstract:

Laser-cooled ions confined in electromagnetic traps provide a unique, tunable mesoscopic system where the interplay of the trapping potential, nonlinear Coulomb interactions, and laser-ion scattering generates rich, collective dynamics. In this work, we engineer thermally activated switching between…

method: Experimental and theoretical analysis of laser-cooled ions in a pyramidal Coulomb cluster, measuring switching rates and comparing with Kramers-Langer theory.
result: The observed switching rates agree with Kramers-Langer theory, demonstrating symmetry-controlled thermal activation.
conclusion: The work provides a test of Kramers-Langer theory in a mesoscopic ion system, but is not directly relevant to quantum information thermodynamics or the researcher's core interests.

title: Mixed Phases In Feedback Ising Models
authors: Yi-Ping Ma, Ivan Sudakow, And P. L. Krapivsky
abstract:

We study mean-field Ising models in which the coupling depends on the magnetization via a feedback function. We identify mixed phases (MPs) and show that they can be stable at zero temperature for sufficiently strong feedback. Moreover, stable MPs are always superstable, meaning that perturbations d…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 027101] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies mean-field Ising models with feedback-dependent coupling, identifying stable mixed phases at zero temperature.

method: Analytical and numerical analysis of mean-field Ising models with a feedback function coupling to magnetization.
result: Mixed phases are stable at zero temperature for sufficiently strong feedback and are superstable against perturbations.
conclusion: Feedback can stabilize mixed phases in Ising models, which may have implications for nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.

title: Dynamic Scaling Near The Kasteleyn Transition In Spin Ice: Critical Relaxation Of Monopoles And Strings Following A Field Quench
authors: Sukla Pal And Stephen Powell
abstract:
Author(s): Sukla Pal and Stephen Powell

We study dynamics in classical spin ice following a magnetic field quench to close to the Kasteleyn transition, using Monte Carlo simulations and dynamic scaling theory to characterize the relaxation of the magnetization and the density of magnetic monopoles. We have previously argued that this dyna…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 024402] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamic scaling near the Kasteleyn transition in classical spin ice, focusing on relaxation of monopoles and strings after a field quench.
motivation: Understanding the critical dynamics of spin ice systems, particularly the relaxation of topological defects like monopoles, is important for non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
method: Monte Carlo simulations and dynamic scaling theory are used to characterize magnetization and monopole density relaxation after a magnetic field quench.
result: The relaxation exhibits dynamic scaling with exponents consistent with the Kasteleyn transition universality class.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the non-equilibrium dynamics of spin ice, but the system is classical and the focus is on condensed matter physics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Observation Of Non-Hermitian Topology In Cold Rydberg Quantum Gases
authors: Jun Zhang, Ya-Jun Wang, Shi-Yao Shao, Bang Liu, Li-Hua Zhang, Zheng-Yuan Zhang, Xin Liu, Chao Yu, Qing Li, Han-Chao Chen, Yu Ma, Tian-Yu Han, Qi-Feng Wang, Jia-Dou Nan, Yi-Ming Yin, Dong-Yang Zhu, Qiao-Qiao Fang, Dong-Sheng Ding, And Bao-Sen Shi

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to analyze neural network activity.
motivation: Understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate activity is crucial for explaining perception, thought, and action.
method: The authors review recent progress in connecting maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to experimental recordings of thousands of neurons.
result: These methods uncover reproducible behaviors and demonstrate that abstract theoretical principles can have predictive power in neuroscience.
conclusion: Statistical physics provides a quantitative bridge between neural data and theoretical models, advancing our understanding of brain function.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated materials, which may reveal novel phases and functionalities.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways using static or periodic fields.
result: Key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and emergence of metastable states with superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders are identified.
conclusion: Photoexcitation provides a powerful tool to manipulate Mott insulators, but the work is primarily a materials physics review without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics of information processing.

title: Low-frequency Electric Field Sensing With A Rydberg Beam
authors: Jeremy Glick, John R. Dickson, Josie Wood, And Paul Kunz
abstract:
Author(s): Jeremy Glick, John R. Dickson, Josie Wood, and Paul Kunz

The authors perform low-frequency electric field sensing using ionization detection on a collimated beam of Rydberg atoms. This reduces challenges associated with electric field screening effects present in warm vapor cells containing alkali-metal atoms.


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012608] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates low-frequency electric field sensing using a Rydberg atom beam to avoid screening effects in vapor cells.
motivation: Low-frequency electric field sensing with Rydberg atoms is limited by electric field screening in warm vapor cells; a beam approach mitigates this.
method: A collimated beam of Rydberg atoms is used, and ionization detection measures the electric field.
result: The beam method reduces screening effects and enables low-frequency field sensing.
conclusion: Rydberg atom beams offer a practical platform for low-frequency electric field sensing.

tldr: This paper studies the effect of an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg perturbation on the toric code, revealing a quantum phase transition from topological order to a trivial paramagnet.
motivation: Understanding the stability of topological order under perturbations is crucial for quantum error correction and condensed matter physics.
method: The authors use neural-network quantum states (NQS) to compute ground states of the perturbed toric code Hamiltonian for various perturbation strengths.
result: They find a first-order quantum phase transition at a critical perturbation strength, beyond which the system enters a trivial paramagnetic phase.

title: Anyon-induced non-Hermitian Topological Phases
authors: Yi-An Wang, Kun Ding, Linhu Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that anyonic exchange statistics can activate non-Hermitian point-gap topology in models that are topologically trivial in its absence. The emergent topology oscillates more rapidly with the statistical phase as the anyon number increases, and exhibits a parity dependence on the particle number. A perturbative analysis reveals the mechanism: fractional statistics induces a mismatch between momentum terms that, combined with sublattice-dependent dissipation, produces particle-number-dependent non-reciprocity and complex spectral winding. As these effects rely on the formation and exchange of interaction-bound anyons, our results establish exchange statistics as a resource for enabling non-Hermitian topology under programmed dissipation.
tldr: Anyonic exchange statistics can induce non-Hermitian topological phases in otherwise trivial models.
motivation: To explore whether fractional statistics can serve as a resource for generating non-Hermitian topology.
method: The authors analyze models with anyonic statistics and sublattice-dependent dissipation, using perturbative analysis to show that statistics induces non-reciprocity and complex spectral winding.
result: Non-Hermitian point-gap topology emerges, oscillating with statistical phase and depending on anyon number parity.
conclusion: Exchange statistics can enable non-Hermitian topology under programmed dissipation, establishing a new connection between anyons and topological phases.

title: Operator-frame Geometry Of Non-compact Quantum Systems With Frame-vacuum Phase Transitions
authors: Satoshi Tanaka, Gonzalo Ordonez, Masatoshi Kubota, Hiroto Nakano, Kazuki Kanki
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate the geometric structure of non-compact bosonic quantum systems in regimes where vacuum instability renders the relevant quantum states non-normalizable, causing conventional state-space quantum geometry -- described by the Berry connection, curvature, and quantum metric -- to become ill-defined. To overcome this breakdown, we develop a formulation of quantum geometry at the level of canonical operator frames, allowing for complexified Bogoliubov-Valatin transformations that lift the requirement that creation operators be Hermitian conjugates of annihilation operators. Canonical operator frames are defined as choices of bosonic creation and annihilation operators realizing the canonical commutation relations. A natural equivalence relation among such frames generalizes the phase ambiguity of quantum states and determines a parameter space that analytically extends the stable-regime parameter space. The space of canonical operator frames forms a principal bundle over parameter space -- the operator-frame bundle -- equipped with a natural Ehresmann connection that defines parallel transport while preserving the canonical commutation relations. In the stable regime, this construction reduces to the Berry connection, while more generally it yields a well-defined operator-space quantum geometric tensor (QGT) that remains valid across vacuum instabilities. Using the framework of rigged Hilbert spaces, we define a notion of quantum frame vacuum and obtain a consistent state-space QGT. Focusing on a single bosonic mode, we demonstrate analyticity of the QGT across the quantum frame-vacuum phase transition and present the corresponding phase diagram on the complexified squeezing-parameter plane. We further introduce a realistic physical setting that allows continuous paths connecting stable and unstable regimes, along which the QGT evolves smoothly across Stokes lines.
tldr: Develops a geometric formulation for non-compact bosonic quantum systems across vacuum instabilities using operator frames.
motivation: Conventional quantum geometry breaks down when vacuum instability leads to non-normalizable states; a new framework is needed to describe geometric properties across phase transitions.
method: Introduces canonical operator frames with complexified Bogoliubov-Valatin transformations, constructs an operator-frame bundle with an Ehresmann connection, and uses rigged Hilbert spaces to define quantum frame vacua.
result: Obtains a well-defined operator-space quantum geometric tensor that remains analytic across vacuum instabilities, and demonstrates the phase diagram for a single bosonic mode.
conclusion: The operator-frame geometry provides a consistent description of quantum geometry in non-compact systems with vacuum phase transitions, extending Berry connection concepts.

title: Four Classes Of Few-weight Self-orthogonal Codes And Their Applications For Lcd Codes And Quantum Codes
authors: Yue Huang, Zhonghao Liang, Chenlu Jia, Yongkang Wan, Qunying Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since self-orthogonal codes, few-weight codes, linear complementary dual codes(LCD codes, for short) and quantum codes have nice applications in coding theory and cryptography, they have received continuous attention. In 2024, by introducing the notion of the augment code, Heng et al.[30] constructed several classes of few-weight self-orthogonal codes basing on defining sets, which are introduced by Ding et al.[10] in 2007. In this manuscript, for two classes of defining sets, we consider the corresponding augmented codes, construct a class of projective four-weight self-orthogonal codes and three classes of four-weight self-orthogonal codes. And for two classes of these four-weight self-orthogonal linear codes, we determine the parameters of their dual codes. As applications, we construct two classes of LCD codes and a class of quantum codes. In particular, we prove that there exists a class of these LCD codes whose dual codes are almost optimal LCD codes according to the sphere packing bound, and a class of quantum codes are AMDS according to the quantum Singleton bound.
tldr: This paper constructs several classes of few-weight self-orthogonal codes and uses them to derive LCD codes and quantum codes.
motivation: Self-orthogonal codes, few-weight codes, LCD codes, and quantum codes have applications in coding theory and cryptography, motivating the construction of new families.
method: The authors define augmented codes based on two classes of defining sets, construct four-weight self-orthogonal codes, and determine parameters of their duals.
result: They obtain two classes of LCD codes (one with almost optimal duals) and a class of AMDS quantum codes.
conclusion: The constructed codes provide new examples of few-weight self-orthogonal codes with applications to LCD and quantum codes.

title: Gap-Majority Lemmas In Communication Complexity
authors: Huacheng Yu Pachara Sawettamalya
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove an information-theoretically optimal in the two-player randomized communication model. For a base function [MATH], its [MATH]-fold , denoted [MATH], takes [MATH] inputs [MATH] and distinguishes whether [MATH] is at least [MATH] or at most [MATH]. We show that if computing [MATH] with success probability [MATH] requires [MATH] bits of information, then computing [MATH] with success probability [MATH] requires [MATH] bits of information. This result is asymptotically optimal in two aspects: it achieves the correct linear scaling of information cost and the correct constant-constant tradeoff between error rates. This makes [MATH], to our knowledge, only the third explicit outer gadget that admits a strong composition theorem in the two-player communication setting, following the identity and XOR gadgets. From an application side, our gap-majority lemma can be viewed as a generic amplification tool that lifts the hardness of deciding [MATH] into the hardness of approximating [MATH]. tldr: This paper proves an information-theoretically optimal gap-majority lemma for two-player randomized communication complexity, with applications to streaming lower bounds.
motivation: Understanding the composition of communication problems is fundamental to proving lower bounds in communication complexity and streaming algorithms.
method: The authors prove a composition theorem for the gap-majority function, showing that the information cost of the composed function scales linearly with the number of copies, with optimal constant tradeoffs.
result: They achieve an asymptotically optimal gap-majority lemma, making gap-majority the third explicit outer gadget with a strong composition theorem, and use it to derive a tight streaming lower bound for triangle counting.
conclusion: The gap-majority lemma provides a generic amplification tool for lifting hardness of decision problems to approximation problems, with applications in communication complexity and streaming.

method: Uses multiple quantum sensors and a noise mitigation protocol inspired by quantum error correction to reduce individual sensor noise.
result: The protocol suppresses excitation noise, improving the signal-to-noise ratio for wavelike dark matter detection.
conclusion: Quantum error correction techniques can be adapted to enhance quantum sensor performance in fundamental physics experiments.

method: The authors use numerical simulations of few-particle dynamics and analytical methods to study the anyon-Hubbard model mapped to an extended Bose-Hubbard ladder with density-dependent hopping and synthetic gauge flux.
result: They observe asymmetric and chiral dynamics, including directional propagation and density-dependent effects, due to the interplay of anyonic statistics and synthetic gauge fields.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A review of exactly solvable quantum many-body dynamics using space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; this review aims to provide a unified pedagogical view using space-time duality.
method: The review focuses on discretizing time evolution in lattice systems, treating space and time on the same footing, and relating to brickwork quantum circuits.
result: It presents a unified framework for understanding dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems via space-time duality.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful analogy with quantum computation for solving many-body dynamics.

title: A Term-Rewriting Semantics For Pure Quantum States
authors: Dan-Adrian German
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2017, Terry Rudolph introduced an elementary rewriting system that relies on a representation of quantum states as misty states to accurately describe the basics of quantum circuits and quantum computation to high-school and middle-school students. The accessibility and effectiveness of the system are remarkable: every calculation can be done to good-enough accuracy, and perhaps with a small overhead, using just a tiny, universal set of gates chosen to take advantage of a remarkable mathematical result by Yaoyun Shi, leveraging another powerful result by A. Y. Kitaev. The misty formalism greatly simplifies calculations and makes them accessible to first-time learners using only simple arithmetic, and without sacrificing accuracy; it, too, is universal, inasmuch as you can use it to do any quantum calculation with maybe just a small overhead. We don't advocate that we should recast all of quantum theory into this formalism. The misty state picture is a good way of getting people to the heart of some nontrivial quantum theory without having to first absorb a huge amount of (what might initially seem largely) irrelevant math. Our argument is that the misty formalism can effectively be used to facilitate a transition to the full, conventional quantum-mathematical apparatus. To this end, we start by reviewing the original proposal, consider its strengths and limitations, and show it in action via entanglement swapping. We then extend the formalism through a new category of (irreducible) misty states acting as fixed points, and present the GHZ game in this new, general setting and representational semantics.
tldr: This paper extends Terry Rudolph's misty state formalism for teaching quantum computing to a more general rewriting semantics with irreducible misty states.
motivation: The misty formalism makes quantum calculations accessible to beginners, but its original version has limitations. The authors aim to extend it to handle more complex scenarios like the GHZ game.
method: The paper reviews the original misty state rewriting system, identifies its strengths and limitations, then introduces a new category of irreducible misty states as fixed points, and applies the extended formalism to the GHZ game.
result: The extended formalism can represent entanglement swapping and the GHZ game using the new irreducible misty states, providing a more general representational semantics.
conclusion: The misty formalism, while not intended to replace standard quantum theory, can serve as a pedagogical bridge to full quantum mechanics, and the extensions improve its expressiveness.

title: Unified Framework For Binary-Choice Dynamics: Analysis And Applications
authors: Jos\'e F. F. Mendes Arkadiusz J\k{e}drzejewski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate how the unified framework for binary-choice dynamics can be used to study the role of annealed and quenched disorders in homogeneous and heterogeneous systems. The framework defines the structure of interactions between agents without imposing their functional forms. Such a high level of generality allows us to connect many different models across disciplines and find universal rules that apply to all of them. Within this framework, agents update their states under the influence of two competing mechanisms chosen according to individual preferences. We review the literature to classify existing models as homogeneous or heterogeneous based on their preference distribution, and we discuss the role of annealed (changing) and quenched (fixed) disorders in modeling these preferences. Using the framework, we derive a constraint on the transition rates. When a model meets this condition, three major things happen: annealed and quenched dynamics become equivalent, any heterogeneous system can be mapped into a homogeneous one, and oscillations cannot emerge. We illustrate these consequences using models from statistical physics, opinion dynamics, and disease spreading. Finally, we discuss the framework limitations and its potential further developments.
tldr: A unified framework for binary-choice dynamics is presented, connecting models across statistical physics, opinion dynamics, and disease spreading.
motivation: To provide a general framework that unifies various binary-choice models and reveals universal constraints on their dynamics.
method: The framework defines interaction structures without imposing functional forms, and derives a constraint on transition rates that leads to equivalence between annealed and quenched dynamics.
result: When the constraint is met, annealed and quenched dynamics become equivalent, heterogeneous systems map to homogeneous ones, and oscillations are suppressed.
conclusion: The framework offers a powerful tool for analyzing binary-choice systems across disciplines, with clear limitations and potential extensions.

title: Explaining The Magnitude Of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity Via Electron-electron Exchange
authors: Alex J. W. Thom Bence Csakany
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiral molecular structure can couple to electron spin, leading to unexpected spin polarization effects. This Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) was first reported for DNA molecules adsorbed on gold but its microscopic origin remains unclear. We demonstrated though simulation that the exchange arising from electron-electron Coulomb interactions within the self-consistent mean field (Hartree--Fock) approximation can yield significant ([MATH]) spin polarisation for [MATH]-methylcyclohexanone adsorbed on Cu(111) amplifying a much smaller ([MATH]) initial bias, consistent with experiment. Symmetry considerations ensure the result is physically meaningful, while its ab-initio nature ensures all parameters are physically realistic. This amplification is connected to existing studies on spin-symmetry breaking in Hartree--Fock, providing a new pathway for understanding the magnitude of CISS as an emergent phenomenon of interacting electrons.
tldr: This paper uses Hartree-Fock simulations to explain the magnitude of chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) via electron-electron exchange.
motivation: The microscopic origin of CISS remains unclear; this work aims to explain the large spin polarization observed in experiments.
method: The authors perform ab initio Hartree-Fock simulations of 3-methylcyclohexanone adsorbed on Cu(111), incorporating electron-electron exchange interactions.
result: They find that exchange interactions amplify a small initial spin bias to significant spin polarization, consistent with experimental observations.
conclusion: CISS can be understood as an emergent phenomenon of interacting electrons, with exchange interactions playing a key role.

title: Beyond Silica Assumptions: Optical Network Design In The Hollow-Core Era
authors: Zhiping Jiang Md Ghulam Saber
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hollow-core fiber (HCF) is often presented as a modestly improved transmission medium that can be inserted into networks originally designed for solid-core silica. We argue instead that recent progress -- most notably the reported attenuation below 0.1 dBkm[MATH], together with a broad low-loss window, reduced propagation delay, and extremely low optical nonlinearity -- makes it timely to reconsider which long-standing design conventions are fundamental to optical communication and which are specific to silica fiber. By reviewing implications at the physical-layer, transceiver, and network-architecture levels, we suggest that the most durable benefits of HCF may arise not from its use as a drop-in replacement, but from cross-layer co-design. We also outline the studies and experimental demonstrations needed to determine where such advantages are genuinely achievable.
tldr: This paper discusses the potential of hollow-core fiber to replace solid-core silica fiber in optical networks, focusing on physical-layer and network-architecture implications.
motivation: Recent progress in hollow-core fiber (HCF) technology, including low attenuation and low nonlinearity, suggests it may offer benefits beyond a simple drop-in replacement for silica fiber.
method: The authors review implications of HCF at the physical-layer, transceiver, and network-architecture levels, and propose cross-layer co-design as a way to fully exploit HCF advantages.
result: The paper argues that the most durable benefits of HCF may come from rethinking network design conventions rather than using HCF as a direct substitute.
conclusion: Further studies and experimental demonstrations are needed to determine where the advantages of HCF are genuinely achievable.

title: Exoplanet Detection Using Adaptive Quantum-Optimal Measurement
authors: Hyunsoo Choi, Hyoung Won Baac, Zubin Jacob, Haejun Chung
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting terrestrial exoplanets in the habitable zones of nearby stars remains a critical challenge. Such planets can be \(10^8\) to \(10^{10}\) times fainter than their host stars and lie at diffraction-limited angular separations, where starlight strongly obscures the companion signal. Here we present an adaptive quantum measurement method for estimating the number, positions, and brightnesses of mutually incoherent point sources in the sub-Rayleigh, ultra-high-contrast regime, operating at contrasts down to \(10^{-8}\) -- five orders of magnitude beyond previous quantum imaging approaches to exoplanet detection. The method adopts a spatial-mode basis that is updated to maximize the quantum Fisher information per detected photon. Estimation is performed by maximum likelihood in log-brightness coordinates, and the source count is determined by Bayesian-information-criterion (BIC) model selection directly from photon-count statistics, without a tunable detection threshold. For point sources within sub-Rayleigh separations and with brightness ratios spanning eight orders of magnitude, the method reconstructs complete scenes with a mean success rate of \(72.5\%\). Furthermore, it is robust to misalignment, maintaining a \(71.3\%\) success rate under offsets of up to six pixels. These results demonstrate that terrestrial exoplanets can be detected below the Rayleigh limit, a regime previously inaccessible to direct imaging.
tldr: This paper presents an adaptive quantum measurement method for detecting exoplanets in the sub-Rayleigh, ultra-high-contrast regime.
motivation: Detecting terrestrial exoplanets in habitable zones is challenging due to extreme faintness and angular separation. Existing direct imaging methods are limited by the Rayleigh criterion.
method: The method uses a spatial-mode basis updated to maximize quantum Fisher information per photon, with maximum likelihood estimation in log-brightness coordinates and Bayesian model selection for source count.
result: The method achieves detection at contrasts down to 10^{-8}, five orders of magnitude beyond previous quantum imaging approaches, with a mean success rate of 72.5% for sub-Rayleigh separations.
conclusion: Terrestrial exoplanets can be detected below the Rayleigh limit, opening a previously inaccessible regime for direct imaging.

title: Invariant Measures For Soliton Systems Generated By Mealy Automata
authors: Yutaro Nakabayashi Takahiro Kanazawa
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study invariant measures for soliton systems described by Mealy automata. Motivated by recently introduced soliton models associated with 2-letter, 3-state Mealy automata, we formulate the time evolution induced by Mealy automata on bi-infinite configuration spaces. We provide sufficient conditions for the invariance of Bernoulli product measures and derive a criterion for the invariance of two-sided space-homogeneous Markov distributions. We then apply these general results to three soliton models, which can be interpreted as variants of the box-ball system (BBS). For two of these models, BBS-S(2) and BBS-V(2), we prove that Bernoulli product measures are invariant. For the remaining model, BBS-C(2), we establish a more general result: the invariance of two-sided space-homogeneous Markov distributions, which include Bernoulli product measures as a special case. Furthermore, for all three models, we compute the phase shift associated with the interaction of two solitons, as well as the velocity of an isolated soliton. Although the latter has already been studied previously, both quantities constitute fundamental characteristics for understanding the generalized hydrodynamics of these systems. These results provide a foundation for the study of invariant measures, generalized Gibbs ensembles, and generalized hydrodynamic behavior in Mealy-automaton soliton systems.
tldr: This paper studies invariant measures for soliton systems generated by Mealy automata, focusing on Bernoulli and Markov distributions.
motivation: To understand the statistical properties and generalized hydrodynamics of soliton systems described by Mealy automata.
method: Formulates time evolution on bi-infinite configuration spaces, provides sufficient conditions for invariance of Bernoulli product measures and Markov distributions, and applies to three soliton models.
result: Proves invariance of Bernoulli measures for two models and invariance of Markov distributions for a third model; computes phase shifts and soliton velocities.
conclusion: The results lay groundwork for studying invariant measures and generalized hydrodynamics in Mealy-automaton soliton systems.

title: Single-laser Stimulated Brillouin Scattering Microscopy
authors: Feihong Lin, Zechao Wen, Jiahui Li, Xiaoyu Yang, Haonan Zhang, Jiahe Zhang, Peiqing Zhang, Xu Liu, Qing Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) microscopy enables label-free mapping of local viscoelastic properties, but frequency-domain implementations are often limited by uncertainty in the pump-probe frequency-difference axis. We demonstrate an RF-defined single-laser electro-optic-modulation SBS microscope in which the pump and probe are derived from the same optical carrier and their frequency difference is set by an electro-optically generated sideband. This architecture makes laser-frequency noise largely common mode and eliminates optical wavelength tuning during spectral scanning. It achieves Brillouin frequency shift and linewidth precisions of 0.07 MHz and 0.30 MHz, respectively. Comparison with a low-NA reference linewidth indicates a system-level spectral broadening of approximately 3.1 MHz, corresponding to an effective spectral resolution of approximately 3 MHz. Imaging of femtosecond-laser-modified chalcogenide glass resolves MHz-level Brillouin contrasts corresponding to 10^-4-level apparent longitudinal-modulus contrast. This work demonstrates the feasibility of transferring the frequency definition of SBS spectral scanning from optical wavelength tuning to RF-domain control, providing a new conceptual and technical basis for high-precision, high-spectral-fidelity Brillouin imaging.
tldr: This paper presents a single-laser stimulated Brillouin scattering microscopy technique for high-precision viscoelastic imaging.
motivation: Frequency-domain SBS microscopy suffers from uncertainty in pump-probe frequency difference and laser frequency noise.
method: The authors use an electro-optic modulator to generate sidebands from a single laser, making the frequency difference RF-defined and common-mode noise canceling.
result: They achieve Brillouin frequency shift and linewidth precisions of 0.07 MHz and 0.30 MHz, with an effective spectral resolution of ~3 MHz.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a new RF-domain frequency definition approach for high-precision Brillouin imaging.

title: Absolute Frequency Measurement Of The $^{176}$Lu$^+\,(^{3}\mathrm{D}_1)$ Standard Against The NRC-FCs2 Fountain With $2.6\times10^{-16}$ Uncertainty
